notes.title: Once upon a time and a very good time it was there was a moocow
notes.html_source:
The story opens with Stephen Dedalus as a young child being told a story by his father. Since the text focuses on Stephen, Joyce presents the reader not only with what Stephen can remember, but also how he remembers it. The narrative voice mimics the childish perception: it is written as free indirect discourse.

As the novel progresses, such syntax and vocabulary dissipates with Stephen’s growth.

Fun fact: According to Urban Dictionary, moocows are different from regular cows.

notes.title: He hid under the table
notes.html_source:
Rewriting his own earlier ‘epiphany’:

Bray: in the parlour of the house in Martello Terrace.
Mr Vance (comes in with a stick): “…O, you know, he’ll have to apologise, Mrs Joyce.”
Mrs Joyce: “O yes… Do you hear that, Jim?”
Mr Vance: “Or else– if he doesn’t the eagles’ll come and pull out his eyes.”
Mrs Joyce: “O, but I’m sure he will apologise.”
Joyce (under the table, to himself):

“Pull out his eyes,
Apologise,
Apologise,
Pull out his eyes.

Apologise,
Pull out his eyes,
Pull out his eyes,
Apologise."

Joyce denies us any hint of what he’d done wrong.

By repeating the rhyme, he embeds this traumatic association deeper into his unconscious.

It is significant that he would reference the song as the title fits well with all the discussion around lavender and roses, but the part about disease is also telling. Is it foreshadowing? Is it ironic?

It seems almost too coincidental that he is now exhibiting signs of gluttony in the way he is longing for large amounts of food. Both of these situations feature one of the seven deadly sins recognized by the Christian church, and they depict Stephen’s descent from the graces of God into the world of sin. Similarly, it can be argued that Stephen’s hunger causes him to fetishize food in a sinful manner.

notes.title: Could it be? He knelt there sinless and timid; and he would hold upon his tongue the host and God would enter his purified body
notes.html_source: In order to demonstrate the development of Stephen’s consciousness Joyce ends each chapter with an epiphany. Stephen recognizes the delusion of one way of life and recognizes the truth of another. In this moment Stephen understands that he must turn to a religious life. Unlike other novels where the narrators look back at the events of their childhood with an adult outlook, Portrait takes up a different style. When Stephen declares, “Another life!” and “The past was past,” we are given no hints that Stephen’s religious life will eventually be replaced by his artistic life. Rather, much like Stephen, we are led to believe that he will remain religious for the rest of his life. In this sense, we experience the successive epiphanies in Stephen’s life just as he experiences them.

notes.title: When the soul of a man is born in this country there are nets flung at it to hold it back from flight. You talk to me of nationality, language, religion. I shall try to fly by those nets
notes.html_source:
There are two interpretations for what this passage could mean, specifically the third last word: “by”.

The obvious is that Dedalus will try to “fly” past the nets of “nationality, language, and religion” which have restrained him or his “soul” since birth. He will fly by them in that he will evade and escape them, flourishing as an artist and a person in spite of their restrictive powers.

However, there is an alternative understanding of this phrase. Dedalus could mean that he intends to fly by these nets in that it is by use of nets that he will fly. It will not be in spite of, but with these nets which have constrained him all of his life that he will soar above his entrapment.
This is implicit in the way in which Dedalus has grown as a writer and as a person throughout the text. His narrative, while it has grown past the restrictions of his surroundings, does so entirely through them. Later on in the chapter Cranly remarks “dispassionately”: “It is a curious thing, do you know… how your mind is supersaturated with the religion in which you disbelieve.” This is accurate: while Dedalus entirely rejects his religious upbringing his use of language and his way of thinking are irreversibly coloured by it. Similarly his nationality and his culture have molded him and his art irreversibly.
Through this interpretation of the statement, Dedalus is claiming that he will transcend as a spirit not in spite of his upbringing but with it. It is “by” or because of that which once tied him down that he will ascend.
